concept.title: The Lead Magnet Title Filter
concept.promise: You can score the title of any lead magnet you are about to publish and predict what share of the downloads will be people you could actually close.
concept.why_this_one:
Your post about the client with the 10,000-name Kit list already has the whole thing in it: you read the title before the asset and run it through three questions, and changing one word took his ICP share from under 2% to 30-40%. That test lives in your head and comes out one sales call at a time, so putting it on a page lets an agency owner run it on their own title tonight without you on the call.

Your buyer has a PDF sitting in a folder and a title they picked in ten seconds, and this gives them a number for it before they publish. They hand over an email because the alternative is finding out after 400 downloads that under 8 of them were worth chasing.
concept.quote: who does it let in, who does it turn away, and of the ones it lets in, what share could you actually close?

outline.heading: What the title decides
outline.what_goes_in: Open with the three questions you run on a title before you read the asset: who it lets in, who it turns away, and of the ones it lets in, what share could you actually close. Make clear the title does the sorting before anyone clicks download, using AI for agencies against AI for paid media agencies as the two versions of the same PDF.

outline.heading: How to score it
outline.what_goes_in: Explain the mechanics in a few lines: five questions, each scored 0, 1 or 2, write the number in the box, total out of 10, then read the band at the end. Tell them to score the title exactly as they would publish it, the version they are already drafting in their head still needs the same treatment.

outline.heading: Does it name your buyer
outline.what_goes_in: Score whether the buyer appears in the title by name, with agency owners scoring above founders and paid media agency owners above agency owners. Give the 0, 1 and 2 descriptions and note the point you make in your post: the more specific name pulls a smaller list with more of the people you would book a call with.

outline.heading: Does it turn anyone away
outline.what_goes_in: Score whether a freelancer three rungs down or a student reads the title and scrolls past on purpose. A title that turns away nobody scores 0, and say plainly that this is the question most titles fail.

outline.heading: Does the problem cost them money
outline.what_goes_in: Score whether the title points at a problem the buyer already has and already pays for: a churned client, a slow month, a retainer that is 40% of revenue. Vague curiosity topics score 0, a problem with a number attached scores 2.

outline.heading: Could you sell to the reader
outline.what_goes_in: Score whether the person the title attracts can buy the service you actually sell, on budget and on authority. Have them check the title against their last five closed clients and mark whether those five would have downloaded it.

outline.heading: Your score and what to do
outline.what_goes_in: Give the bands with the ICP share each one predicts, from the under 2% end to the 30-40% end, and the download math: 400 downloads at under 2% is under 8 worth chasing, at 30-40% it is 120 to 160. Close with the one-word fix instruction, change the narrowest word in the title, rescore, republish the same PDF.

concept.capture_note: Put it on one page on inboundonsteroids.com, the scorecard as a file a reader gets after entering an email address. The list it builds is yours, on your domain, and every name on it told you they are about to publish a lead magnet.

alternates.title: Turn One Quarter Of Calls Into Forty Posts
alternates.promise: You can open your last quarter of call recordings and pull out a named list of post-ready moments without inventing a single take.

alternates.title: Find The Stage Your Outreach Drops
alternates.promise: You can enter your invites, accepts, replies and calls, and see which single stage is losing you the pipeline and what to change there.

concept.buyer: Agency owners doing 6 or 7 figures a year who sell services to other businesses and want LinkedIn to produce booked calls without eating their week. They keep getting stuck on the capture step: they post consistently, collect reactions and comments, and end the quarter with almost no named leads, because the feed reaches everyone and nothing in it asks a reader for an email address.

giveaway_post.body:
An agency owner showed me his feed last week. Three years posting, good comments, steady reactions, almost 0 inbound. His plan was to post more.

The part nobody checks is the title on the thing he was giving away. It decides who raises a hand before anyone reads a word of it.

So I built a scorecard. You put your title in, and it runs the three questions I run before I ever open the asset: who does it let in, who does it turn away, and of the ones it lets in, what share could you actually close?

You score each one, add it up, and the sheet gives you the rough share of downloads that will be people you could book a call with.

There's a fix list in there too, plus the before and after that made me write it.

A client had "AI for agencies." He changed one word, to "AI for paid media agencies," same PDF, same feed, and ICP climbed to 30-40%.

I run this on every title before it goes out. One I run it for has about 40% of his downloads coming back as other agency owners, the exact buyer he sells to.

Score the title first. The topic does the sorting before anyone clicks download.

Comment SCORECARD and I'll send it over.
